title: Latency-Cost Hybrid Routing Playbook
content:
Purpose and context:
This note collects a concrete, implementable playbook for a hybrid routing strategy that balances per-request latency SLOs and provider/hardware cost objectives for Redwood's multi-region inference platform. Aim: prefer local/low-latency regions, fall back to cheaper (but potentially higher-latency) regions when capacity or price constraints require it, and provide predictable control-plane APIs for product teams to opt in/out.

Audience:
- Platform engineers implementing control-plane policies and traffic routers
- Serving/runtime teams implementing region-aware routing hooks
- SREs who operate capacity and incidents

Design constraints and non-goals:
- Must not violate regional data residency requirements (privacy/compliance trumps performance).
- Should be transparent to hosted API customers via metadata/tracing so cost/latency can be attributed per-call.
- Non-goal: global traffic consolidation onto a single cheapest region (we still want geographic locality).

Key concepts and terminology (short):
- Local preference: route to a region that is within latency budget and has available capacity.
- Cost-fallback: if local capacity is insufficient or the local unit-cost exceeds a configured threshold, route to a lower-cost region subject to latency cap.
- Hedging vs. probe-driven: hedging sends duplicate probes to multiple regions to pick the fastest; probe-driven uses periodic measurements to choose likely-best region without duplication.
- Quiet-failover: an automated, gradual shift of traffic during a failover instead of instant cutover to minimize cache churn and hot-shard effects.

Routing policy primitives (control plane knobs):
- region_priority_list: ordered list of candidate regions per tenant/model (string list).
- latency_budget_ms: absolute max p90/p95 latency acceptable for this route (string number stored as string).
- cost_threshold_usd_per_token: preferred max unit cost before considering cheaper regions.
- capacity_reserve_pct: percent of region capacity to keep for local traffic to avoid total bleed to cheaper regions (default 10%).
- fallback_mode: one of [probe-driven, hedging, strict-preference, round-robin-fallback].
- drain_window_seconds: how long to gradually move traffic during planned rebalancing or failure (default 300s).

Decision flow (per-request, simplified):
1) Evaluate local region health: available_capacity >= request_units and recent_probe_latency_p95 <= latency_budget_ms? If yes, route locally.
2) If local fails health checks, consult region_priority_list. For each region in order:
   - check capacity and unit_cost against cost_threshold_usd_per_token
   - ensure latency estimate (from probes) <= latency_budget_ms
   - pick first matching region.
3) If no region matches and fallback_mode is hedging, issue small hedged probe (100ms head-room token) to top-2 candidate regions and pick winner; otherwise return overload or queue depending on tenant SLO.

Telemetry and probing design:
- Active probes: every region pair (client-region -> serving-region) should have a lightweight probe measurement (p50/p90/p99 latencies and packet loss) with an adaptive cadence: high-traffic pairs probed every 15s, low-traffic every 5m.
- Passive signals: attach observed tail latencies from real requests to the probe store. Passive metrics should influence fast path decisions but be smoothed to avoid flapping.
- Cost telemetry: per-region unit cost estimates should be published hourly to the control plane and include GPU instance price + egress cost estimate + any reserved capacity amortization.

Failure and gradual transition mechanics:
- Quiet failover (planned maintenance): control plane will shift up to 10% of traffic per drain_window_seconds step to target region, observing latencies and error rates at each step. If degradation exceeds configured rollback thresholds (error increase > 2x baseline or p95 increase > 20%), abort and revert.
- Unplanned failure: immediate detection triggers a conservative shift: mark region unhealthy and reroute to first healthy candidate but with a short hedged probe to the next candidate to reduce misrouting.

GeoDNS vs Anycast recommendations (practical):
- Use GeoDNS for coarse regional steering and origin selection (region affinity, compliance zones). GeoDNS gives control and visibility but slower TTL-based convergence.
- Use Anycast (via CDN/edge) only for very low-latency front-door where single-hop routing is necessary and we can tolerate blackholing risk; pair Anycast with health-aware BGP or endpoint health-checks.
- Hybrid pattern: GeoDNS chooses the region group; within the region group use an internal Anycast/edge to pick a specific POP. This provides locality while retaining region-level control.

Control plane APIs (proposal):
- GET /routing-policy/{tenant}/{model} -> returns region_priority_list, latency_budget_ms, cost_threshold_usd_per_token, fallback_mode, capacity_reserve_pct.
- POST /routing-policy/{tenant}/{model}/simulate -> accept candidate weights and return simulated latency/cost projection based on recent probe/cost data (for product team experimentation).
- Event hooks: control plane emits ROUTE_CHANGE events to telemetry and observability when a region change occurs for a request higher than threshold.

Operational playbook & runbook snippets:
- Incident: region p95 latency spike > 2x baseline for > 2m -> control-plane mark unhealthy, reroute traffic, notify SRE rotation, open incident.
- Cost alert: rolling 24h unit cost for a tenant > cost_threshold_usd_per_token -> notify account owner and optionally enable temporary auto-fallback to cheaper pool.
- Canary rollout: enable route-policy change for 1% of traffic, measure cost/latency/quality for 1h, then ramp to 10/50/100 with automated gates.

Open questions / tradeoffs to discuss:
- How to price/charge when a request crosses regions (which tenant pays for egress)? We need invoice-level attribution rules.
- Hedging increases egress and compute cost. What explicit budget or guardrails do we offer tenants?
- How aggressive should cost-fallback be for enterprise customers with SLAs? Likely allow per-tenant opt-outs (enforce strict locality).

Action items / next steps:
- (Aisha) Draft control-plane API PR with fields above and simulation endpoint (due 2025-02-01).
- (Miguel) Prototype adaptive probe cadence and store (due 2025-02-14).
- (Evan) Run a small canary using a non-critical model to test quiet-failover steps (due 2025-02-07).
- (Priya) Write billing attribution doc for cross-region requests and egress (due 2025-02-20).

Notes and references:
- Keep logs of per-request chosen-region in trace metadata (x-region, x-routing-reason) so product and SRE can filter.
- For critical tenants allow an "always-local" flag enforced by policy.

Rough appendix: quick heuristics table (example):
- If p95_local < latency_budget and capacity_util_local < 85% -> local (fast path).
- If p95_local > latency_budget but top-2 remote regions p95s within 25% -> probe-driven hedging to top-2 and pick fastest.
- If local cost/unit > cost_threshold AND remote p95 <= latency_budget -> prefer remote.

This is intentionally a working playbook. Expect changes after the first couple canaries. Questions, disagreements, or alternate heuristics add as comments below.
